summary: This work characterizes aging and annealing of Al/AlO$_x$/Al Josephson junctions over 2–3 months under different storage environments and thermal conditions. Aging follows a logarithmic curve where the amplitude is set by fabrication (oxidation parameters) while aging speed is governed by storage conditions, with ambient atmosphere aging 3–5× faster than nitrogen or vacuum storage.
motivation: Precise junction resistance control is essential for large-scale superconducting quantum processors, where wafer-scale $I_c$ variations reach 3% and chip-scale 1–2%. Understanding how storage and post-fabrication annealing affect junction resistance enables optimal frequency tuning and reduces unexpected qubit frequency shifts between measurement and cooldown.
method: Al/AlO$_x$/Al junctions (250 nm × 250 nm, Dolan process) were fabricated on high-resistivity silicon and stored in ambient atmosphere, nitrogen glove box ($<0.01\%$ O$_2$), or vacuum ($\sim 10^{-7}$ mbar). Resistance was monitored via I–V curve slope over 56–85 days. Thermal annealing was performed up to 250°C in N$_2$ and ambient; voltage annealing used alternating $\pm 0.9$ V pulses.
result: Logarithmic aging fits give amplitude parameter $a = 0.21 ± 0.02$ (ambient) vs. $0.15 ± 0.02$ (glove box) and timescale $\tau = 1.2 ± 0.5 \times 10^4$ s (ambient) vs. $4.3 ± 2.2 \times 10^4$ s (glove box). In N$_2$, resistance decreases monotonically up to 250°C; in ambient, resistance increases at 200°C and decreases at 250°C. Minimum achievable resistance equals the initial post-fabrication value, setting a lower limit on tuning range.
